sentences.text: Auroraceratops was a moderate-sized, bipedal dinosaur characterized by bony rugosities on its face and jaw.
Unlike most other neoceratopsians with long, narrow snouts, this animal possessed a shorter and wider snout.
Its skull measured approximately 20 centimeters in length and appeared somewhat flat and wide with a narrower base.
The profile of this short, high, and rounded snout resembles that of a turtle.

The creature had at least two pairs of striated ridges on its simple, nearly cylindrical premaxillary teeth, and paired rugose areas likely covered in keratin were located in front of the eyes and on the jugal.
This dinosaur is notable as the first relatively large ceratopsian found in Asia.
The rugose structures on its head were likely used for inter- and intraspecific interactions, possibly involving social dominance conflicts and mating rituals.
A well-preserved skull was recovered in 2004 from the Gongpoquan Basin and accessioned as CAGS IG-2004-VD-001, which was designated as the holotype for the species named in 2005.
The remains were discovered by geologist Li Daqing in the Mazong Shan area of Gansu Province, north-central China, and presented to researchers at the Fossil Development Research Center.
Further excavations in 2007 yielded at least 50 specimens, and the total count of individuals reached 80 by the end of the 2010 field season.
Remains of around 80 individuals were found in Yujingzi, northwest Gansu, providing a nearly complete skeleton.
A 2019 analysis estimated Auroraceratops was a bipedal animal 1.25 m long, with a hip height of 44 cm and a body mass of 15.5 kg.
Evidence suggests Auroraceratops died by rapid burial inside burrows, indicated by curled-up preservation and lack of weathering.
Auroraceratops is classified within the infraorder Ceratopsia and belongs to the class Ornithischia.
The taxon belongs to the unranked family Neoceratopsia, a group defined by the fusion of the first three cervical vertebrae.
Authors determined that Auroraceratops is a taxon sister to Coronosauria, considered the node between Protoceratopsidae and Ceratopsoidea.
In 2015, VanBuren et al. placed Auroraceratops in a third group, consecutive but outside the clade formed by ceratopsians after Protoceratops and Leptoceratops.
Auroraceratops remains were found in Lower Cretaceous sediments of the Xinminpu Formation in the Gongpoquan Basin, Mazong Shan, Gansu Province, northeast China.
During the Albian stage, from 113.2 to 110.1 million years ago, the region where Auroraceratops lived had a fairly dry subtropical climate.
Auroraceratops is found in the red beds of the Zhonggou Formation alongside Archaeoceratops oshimai, Beishanlong, Suzhousaurus, and an unnamed ornithomimosaur.
